# tgt   citation form: singular noun, infinitive verb, masculine
#       singular adjective, nominative singular for Latin/Old English.
# tgt2  plural for nouns, present participle for verbs. A blank tgt2 on
#       a noun means the English plural is never woven, which is the
#       correct outcome: weaving a singular target under an English
#       plural teaches a form that does not exist.
# West Saxon, roughly 900-1050, in the normalised spelling of teaching editions.
# Old English is the best case this whole method has. The target word is very
# often the literal ancestor of the English word it replaced: hus for house,
# stan for stone, cyning for king. The tooltip says so, which turns each swap
# from "memorise this foreign word" into "here is where your word came from".
# The false friends are marked in the note column, because they are the most
# memorable thing in the language: OE "dream" means joy and music, not a
# sleeping vision. "steorfan" means simply to die, and became "starve".
# "sellan" means to give. "faest" means firm, whence both "fast" and
# The etymon column names the English word this one became, and that is a
# claim about the English word, so the English word is where it is checked.
# A translation is not an ancestor: "window" is Old Norse "vindauga", which
# too. Nor is a compound the word itself: "bishopric" contains "rice", but
# "rice" did not become it. Every etymon names the dictionary entry it was
# tests/tools/etymons.test.ts fails on one that names none.
# One spelling is sometimes two words. hund is a dog and a hundred, earm an
# arm and poor, rīċe a realm and rich, and English Wiktionary gives each
# pair two etymologies. A memory card is keyed by the target, so the second
# word of each is written with a homograph number, "hund²", and is a card, a
# page and a ledger key of its own; nothing a reader sees prints the number.
# The first word is written bare, so its card keeps the id it already had.
# The numbers follow Wiktionary's numbering of the etymologies, as all three
# happen to allow; where the two ever disagree, the word that already has
# the card stays bare. "sōþ", true and truth, is one word with one etymology
# tests/tools/lexicon-homographs.test.ts fails on a target shared across
# parts of speech that is neither numbered nor listed there as one word.
